rss_1_1789244479.title: NSF moves to overhaul funding approach in line with White House priorities
rss_1_1789244479.text:
The US National Science Foundation might cut back on its core research grants in favour of those driven by the priorities of US President Donald Trump. Credit: Tada Images/Shutterstock

The US National Science Foundation (NSF) is changing how it funds research grants — and how it decides which ones to fund — to better align with White House priorities, according to a letter released on 10 September.

“NSF is taking decisive action to meet this moment, introducing new and ambitious ideas that capitalize on the changes in the scientific ecosystem to advance our core mission,” says the letter. It is signed by Brian Stone, who is standing in as the NSF’s director.

NSF plans cuts to core science programmes to fund White House initiative

Since its inception in 1950, the NSF, a major funder of basic research, has solicited proposals on topics informed heavily by the scientific community. The letter describes a shift to a “portfolio-based” approach to making grants that combines traditional “investigator-driven inquiry” with “NSF-directed opportunities”. The letter does not say what the opportunities will be, but states that the NSF will specify objectives but “never the method scientists must use” to achieve them.

Staff members at the agency, who spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retaliation, are concerned that the changes will lead to further cuts for work that has long been core to the agency’s mission: discovery-focused research, led by the curiosity of scientists.

When asked for comment on criticisms of the changes, an NSF spokesperson directed Nature to Stone’s letter.

The announcement is the latest in a stream of changes at the NSF instigated by the administration of US President Donald Trump. The administration has prioritized research on artificial intelligence and argued for fundamental changes to who receives research funding and how, while attempting to cut federal science budgets and give political officials more say in grant decisions.

At the frontier

The letter says that solicitations for grant proposals will be “consolidated” and “simplified”. Calls for proposals will also be designed with a greater focus on advancing “a specific aspect of NSF’s mission”, the letter adds.

Central to the NSF’s portfolio-based approach are four research topics that will receive funding from across the agency’s directorates and will also require “cooperation across disciplines and directorates” the letter says. It names four “Frontier Initiatives”: the Future of Intelligence, Frontier of Quantum Phenomena, Advanced Materials and Matter, and Foundations of Biological Design.

These initiatives are a brainchild of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), according to earlier reporting by Nature. The letter does not specify how much will be spent on the frontier initiatives, or how they will be funded, but it says that they will “make full use of the agency’s funding mechanisms … including prizes and challenges”. NSF staff have told Nature that some of the money is likely to come out of the US$1 billion in funding that the agency has been holding in a central account instead of allocating it to grants.

AI and quantum science take centre stage under Trump — but with little new proposed funding

Staff members say that the move to fund the frontier initiatives will probably shrink the agency’s core-science funding and divert large sums to White House priorities. “Ordinarily, there would be optimism that these initiatives could further strengthen the agency’s mission,” one staff member says. “The current administration, however, seems intent on undermining science, so naturally there is scepticism about all of this.”

rss_2_1789244481.title: People trust scientists seen to be 'on their side', UK study find
rss_2_1789244481.text:
Protesters call for the public to put stock in scientists at a UK climate march. Credit: Michael Kemp/Alamy

At a time when misinformation is rife and many seem to be questioning scientific evidence, do people really trust scientists? In the United Kingdom, the answer is mostly yes, finds a study led by the Policy Institute at King’s College London and Sense about Science, a charity based in London.

Trust in science: How to build and maintain public support in an era of polarization

Nearly two-thirds (63%) of 4,262 UK adults surveyed said they trust scientists, giving a score of 7 or higher on a zero to ten scale. Only 5% rated their trust at three or below.

To explore what drives trust and distrust of scientists, the researchers used regression modelling to identify factors most strongly associated with trust. The most influential factors were whether respondents felt that scientists are "on the side of people like them" and whether they thought of scientists as open and transparent. Both outweighed perceptions of scientific expertise.

Previous research has shown that benevolence — the idea that researchers care about society and want to do good — is a core pillar of public trust in science1. Now Bobby Duffy, director of the Policy Institute at King’s College London and one of the authors of the UK study, says that the work reveals that trust in scientists was less associated with scientists being eager to work for the good of society in general (12%) and had more to do with whether they are on the side of people like the respondent (21%).

“In a politically divided society, people become much more interested in, ‘What’s in it for me?’” says Duffy.

Where trust falters

When the researchers delved into specific fields, they found that trust declined for scientists working on vaccines, space and climate (see ‘Pockets of trust’). And more people had more confidence in academics (12%) rather than in scientists working in government (42%) and in private companies (34%). Perhaps unsurprisingly, people with little trust in scientists are more likely to think conspiracy theories about climate change, vaccines and the effects of 5G phone towers are true, says the report.

rss_3_1789244482.title: El Niño goes viral — and scientists learn what makes people care about the climate
rss_3_1789244482.text:
Glaciers shape the landscapes of Spitsbergen, an island of Norway’s Svalbard archipelago in the Arctic Ocean.Credit: Arterra/Sven-Erik Arndt/UIG/Getty

As warnings about a potential ‘mega’ El Niño grab headlines and spread through social media, communicators face a familiar challenge: how to persuade people to pay attention to climate risks — and act.

Fighting climate change takes more than data — it needs wonder, love and hope

A study, now published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology, suggests that emotionally engaging forms of communication are more effective than scientific facts alone in motivating climate action1. But messages focused on individual responsibility had little impact — and sometimes backfired.

“Our findings show that merely providing scientific facts is not the best way to communicate on climate-related issues — you need to connect with people,” says co-author Tobias Brosch, a psychologist at the University of Geneva, Switzerland.

“The emotions you feel when you watch a nature documentary, see the Northern Lights or witness the birth of a new animal imbue these events with meaning,” he adds. “They may also drive you to look better after our environment — by volunteering your time, donating or voting for climate-friendly parties.”

Inspiring awe

The study combined and analysed 71 publications, and included at least 216,000 participants who had been involved in experimental tests of the effect of different public communication methods on climate-related behaviours, such as making charity donations or stating intentions to reduce their carbon footprint in later interviews.

“We wanted to integrate all the scientific literature that has evaluated climate-change communication formats, and then look at impacts that interested us, which is climate action, climate-policy support or climate intentions,” says Brosch.

Most of the communication strategies went some way towards prompting climate action. Fact-based messaging — such as explaining the greenhouse-gas effect — increased the likelihood of people engaging with climate efforts. But communications designed to evoke emotions, such as awe at the beauty of nature and fear of the threats it is facing, were among the most successful.

The study shows the pivotal role of stories in communication, says Nicholas Epley, a behavioural scientist at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business in Illinois. “We reason in stories and concrete experiences: facts aren’t nearly as persuasive as individual stories, particularly when there’s distrust,” he says.

The analysis also showed what didn’t work: reminding individuals of their personal responsibility to act on climate change did little to convince people to mobilize, and even produced retaliation. This is consistent with what other initiatives have found. For example, during Earth Hour — a global event run by the WWF charity that recommends everyone turn their lights off for an hour — some organizations turn on all their lights in defiance.

“It possibly creates reactance, mistrust or this over-saturation of ‘oh, come on, now this is also my responsibility?’,” says Brosch. “Whereas the ones that worked went via an emotional pathway – ‘look, this is what’s worth fighting for’.”

Thijs Bouman, an environmental psychologist at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, says that although the study’s effect sizes are relatively small, they can still be meaningful, particularly for large-scale communication activities. “Sometimes governments and decision makers ask for an intervention that will immediately make a substantial change, but this study shows it is obviously very unrealistic,” he says.

rss_4_1789244484.title: Successful early-career scientists rely on network of mentors
rss_4_1789244484.text:
Survey finds that research mentors help junior scientists write publications and grant applications, whereas other types of mentors are helpful for landing a new job.Credit: Thomas Barwick/Getty

The most successful early-career researchers often rely on a network of mentors who each have different roles — from advising on research and grants to making professional introductions and providing emotional support, finds a study of nearly 900 scientists just starting out1.

The findings are consistent with what mentorship scholars and practitioners have long argued: no single mentor can meet all of a trainee’s scientific, professional and psychosocial needs, says Keivan Stassun, an astrophysicist at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee. “It is encouraging to see these patterns emerge so clearly in a large data set of successful early-career investigators,” says Stassun, who has won awards for his mentorship.

For the study, which was posted on the bioRxiv preprint server and hasn’t been peer-reviewed, researchers analysed responses from recipients of K awards, issued by the US National Institutes of Health for career development. These prestigious grants support early-career researchers in strengthening their research skills and provide time for training activities that prepare them to become independent investigators.

The team found that recipients had a median of 3 mentors when they applied for their awards, although some reported as many as 15. More than 90% of the awardees said that mentoring relationships resulted in publications and grants. Other common mentoring outcomes were new professional connections (88.5%) and enhanced skills (81.8%).

The authors acknowledge that although recruitment for the study targeted successful and unsuccessful award applicants, most respondents were recipients. This prevented comparisons of characteristics between those who won awards and those who didn’t, the authors write.

Different outcomes

Participants were asked to categorize their mentors into six predefined roles. All of them had a research mentor, but many others served as coaches, sponsors, connectors or peers. Connectors used their professional network to introduce the early-career researcher to useful contacts, and sponsors used their seniority and influence to advocate for their trainees and help to create opportunities. Some awardees also had an ‘identity mentor’, with whom they shared certain traits, such as gender, race, ethnicity, nationality or sexual orientation.

Different mentor roles were associated with different types of success. For instance, research mentors were most strongly associated with achievements such as writing publications, winning grants and gaining research skills. Psychosocial benefits — such as building confidence, personal growth and improved work–life balance — came from relationships with coaches, peer mentors and identity mentors. And early-career researchers were more likely to land a job because of their relationship with a connector or sponsor than through their research mentor.

This is an important takeaway, says co-author Felicia Setiono, a health-equity researcher at SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University in Brooklyn, New York. Most postdocs aspire to continue in academia, and these positions are competitive, she says. “Yet postdocs still tend to primarily rely on their main research adviser to navigate the process for pursuing their next steps,” she adds.

Under-represented scientists

Roughly 15% of awardees were from groups under-represented in science, and they in particular seem to benefit from larger mentoring networks compared with researchers outside those groups.

rss_5_1789244485.title: Osteoporosis affects millions: could modified cells rebuild their bones?
rss_5_1789244485.text:
Osteoporosis causes thin, porous bones that are prone to fracture, but a promising cell therapy might offer a way to strengthen them.Credit: Dr Tony Brain/SPL

The ten older women had, between them, broken their bones dozens of times, often after little more than a stumble. But after receiving a single infusion of their own bone-marrow cells, treated in the laboratory to help the cells penetrate bone tissue, the women’s fractures all but stopped.

Before treatment, the women — the participants of small clinical trial reported1 today in Cell — experienced fractures in their spines, hips, arms and other bones every year or two, on average. After the trial, the women experienced bone breaks caused by low-impact trauma at a rate closer to once per decade.

The results raise the tantalizing possibility that a one-time cell therapy could rebuild brittle bones in people with osteoporosis, an ageing-related condition that affects around 200 million women worldwide, particularly after menopause.

“It’s quite remarkable,” says Ajit Varki, a physician-scientist at the University of California, San Diego who was not involved in the study. The trial “showed an almost 100% efficacy sustained for several years — and no side effects”.

Still, the findings come with hefty caveats. The study was small, had no control group and most of its participants were taking conventional osteoporosis drugs before and during the trial, making it difficult to tease out the effects of the cell therapy.

What’s more, the researchers did not directly track the therapeutic cells in the recipients’ bodies, leaving a crucial question unanswered: did enough of the cells reach the bones to make a difference?

Straight to the bone

Robert Sackstein, a regenerative-medicine specialist at the Miami Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Florida and a co-author on the study, is confident that they did. Sackstein has spent decades studying how various cells with regenerative potential — including bone-forming progenitor cells known as mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) — can be steered through the body for maximal therapeutic effect.

MSCs, when injected into the bloodstream, cannot usually reach bone tissue. But in 2008, Sackstein and his colleagues found that adding a sugar called fucose to these stem cell-like cells enabled them to seek out and enter bones, leading to skeletal tissue generation in mice2.

Women’s health research lacks funding – these charts show how

The added sugars usually disappear within about two days, and are thought to work by fostering interactions between the MSCs and blood-vessel walls. Those interactions slow the cells, allowing them to squeeze into the bone marrow.

After seeing the approach work in mice, Sackstein and his colleagues turned their attention to humans. According to the authors, few trials had tested MSCs for osteoporosis, and no trials in any disease had deliberately modified the cells to improve their trafficking ability. It took several years to fine-tune the manufacturing process3 and generate the required preclinical data before the trial could proceed.

But finally, in 2015, clinical collaborators in Spain led by bone-marrow transplant specialist José Moraleda at the University of Murcia, began the trial. They treated women aged 51 to 72, who had advanced osteoporosis and a history of fractures, with MSCs extracted from their own bone marrow and enhanced with fucose.

rss_6_1789244487.title: Author Correction: The molecular basis of force selectivity by PIEZO2
rss_6_1789244487.text:
Correction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10182-7 Published online 4 March 2026

In the version of this article initially published, in the Fig. 4d Source Data and associated figure plot, due to an error during the full width at half maximum resolution analysis using the ‘fwhm_on_spots’ jython-fiji macro, one channel from one image was inadvertently loaded twice into the analysis script. The corrected analysis changes the PIEZO2 FWHM from 83 ± 31 nm to 88 ± 32 nm and the number of PIEZO2 puncta from n = 201 to n = 320. The figure panel and Source Data are now updated. In the Fig. 4d legend, the reported n value for FLNB puncta was incorrect and is now updated to n = 468 rather than 469.

In the Source Data for Figs. 1–3, the “Raw MINFLUX output” tabs for cell #2 of the “PIEZO2 TCOK105 – Isotonic” condition contained values from an analysis version that used a different standard-deviation-per-trace threshold from that used for the figures. Separately, in the “Raw MINFLUX output” tab in the Source Data of Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 4 for cell #3 of the “mPIEZO1 TCO*K103 – Hypotonic” condition, an analysis output was uploaded in which two molecules that should have been excluded by the z-axis filtering criterion were inadvertently retained. (The Source Data Extended Data Fig. 4 file was originally mislabeled Source Data Extended Data Fig. 3).

Following the Source Data updates, the Fig. 1b legend now reports n = 102 instead of n = 52 molecules for the unstimulated PIEZO2 condition; Fig. 1d now reports a median of 37.1 nm and n = 39 molecules instead of 34.7 nm and n = 41 molecules; Fig. 1e now reports 20.8 nm instead of 19.9 nm for the unstimulated PIEZO2 condition; the PIEZO2 values in Fig. 3e now report median = 20.8 nm and n = 102 molecules rather than median = 18.0 nm and n = 30 molecules. In the Fig. 1–3 legends, in three cases, mean values were reported rather than the correct median values, where for Fig. 1h, PIEZO1 hyperosmotic condition, 19.8 nm has been updated to 17.1 nm; for Fig. 2b, PIEZO2 + cytochalasin D at rest, 20.1 nm has been updated to 18.0 nm; for Fig. 3e, Flnb DsiRNA + hypo-osmotic swelling, 37.0 nm has been updated to 38.7 nm. In the Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2 legends, sample sizes were listed incorrectly, where for Fig. 1k, PtK2 control cells, n = 6 has been updated to n = 7 cells; for Extended Data Fig. 2d, direct Alexa 647, n = 2,014 has been updated to 2,013 traces, fluorogenic DNA PAINT, n = 7,254 has been updated to 7,253 traces, and for traditional DNA PAINT, n = 1,013 has been updated to 1,012 traces. In the Extended Data Fig. 8c legend, a typographical error in “Piezo2 Flnb KO” has been corrected to “Piezo1 Flnb KO”.

The corrections do not affect the outcome or significance of any reported statistical comparison, the direction of any experimental result, or the scientific conclusions or interpretations presented in the article. Figure 4d, the legends for Figs. 1–4 and Extended Data Figs. 2 and 8, and Source Data for Figs. 1–4 and Extended Data Fig. 4 are now updated in the HTML and PDF versions of the article. For comparison, the original Fig. 4 is available as Supplementary Information accompanying this amendment.

rss_8_1789244489.title: Distant sensors announced a fearsome tsunami’s birth
rss_8_1789244489.text:
Seismic data pinpoint the collapse of an underwater volcano, and reveal how the eruption triggered a destructive tsunami.

Buildings on Tongatapu, the main island of Tonga, were damaged after the eruption of the underwater Hunga volcano in 2022 triggered a series of tsunamis. Credit: Mary Lyn Fonua/Matangi Tonga/AFP/Getty

A powerful volcanic eruption in the South Pacific Ocean has revealed a way to detect a tsunami unleashed by such an event1.

Underwater volcanoes are hard to monitor, mainly because they are hidden in the depths of the ocean. When the submarine Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha‘apai volcano in the island nation of Tonga erupted in January 2022, it triggered tsunamis that struck the coasts of nearby islands with little warning, producing waves more than 40 metres high.

To learn how the 11-hour eruption unfolded, Shane Cronin at the University of Auckland in New Zealand and his colleagues pored over data captured by seismic sensors hundreds to thousands of kilometres away from Hunga. They spotted high-frequency, slow-moving seismic signals known as T-waves, created as the eruption’s energy radiated out into the ocean.

The characteristics of the T-waves showed they were strongest about an hour after the eruption began, when the top of the underwater volcano fractured and collapsed. This collapse also generated the largest and most destructive tsunami of the eruption.

Because T-waves travel at least seven times faster than tsunamis do, they could serve as early warnings of tsunamis generated by underwater eruptions.

rss_10_1789244492.title: Daily briefing: Text-message tutoring keeps kids learning when schools close
rss_10_1789244492.text:
Twenty-minute phone calls from tutors improved children’s maths learning during emergency school closures. Plus, Denisovans made excellent deer hunters and Beatles puns are here, there and everywhere in scientific literature.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

In 2025, researchers used protein analysis to show that a jawbone recovered from ocean sediments off the coast of Taiwan belonged to a Denisovan.Credit: Yousuke Kaifu

A collection of fossils and artefacts recovered from an abandoned quarry in southwestern China has given researchers an unprecedented glimpse into the lives of ancient humans called Denisovans. The items suggest that Denisovans — who lived at the site for at least 30,000 years — crafted bone tools similar to those of the Neanderthals, and were skilled hunters of animals such as deer. “This site’s the full package,” says archaeologist Ben Marwick. “It’s the first site that we have with a long, rich sequence that’s uniquely associated with Denisovans.”

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: Nature paper 1 & paper 2

Text messages and weekly 20-minute phone calls from a teacher can improve children’s learning during prolonged school closures. The approach offers a relatively cheap way to support children’s mathematics education when schooling is disrupted by natural disasters, pandemics or other emergencies, say the study authors. In a trial across five countries, kids that received both texts and phone calls improved the most. But text messages alone also improved children's learning compared to a control group.

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: Nature paper

At least 3,200 The number of titles of peer-reviewed scientific papers that reference the names or lyrics of songs by The Beatles. (Science | 5 min read) Reference: PLOS One paper (the title of which also contains a Beatles pun)

A prototype tool called ProteinTalks can predict how the cells in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) tumours — which can behave very differently at the molecular level — will respond to various drugs. Researchers trained the computational simulation on millions of protein measurements collected over time from breast cancer cell lines that were treated with dozens of antitumour drugs and drug combinations. The model did a good job of predicting how cells would respond to drugs it hadn’t seen before and real-world clinical outcomes.

Nature | 6 min read

Reference: Nature paper

Infographic of the week

The United Nations has voted to phase out use of the Mercator map, a widely used sixteenth-century projection that has been criticized for not representing countries’ sizes accurately. The Mercator map depicts land masses closer to the poles — most of which are in the Northern Hemisphere — as disproportionately large. This can be problematic because people are inclined to conflate size and importance, researchers say. The UN resolution instead endorses use of the Equal Earth projection, which more accurately depicts the relative sizes of land masses. (Nature | 5 min read)

Features & opinion

In 2019, retired topologist Joan Birman received an email from 15-year-old Vasudha Bharathram asking for help in learning geometry. After a few meetings, Birman realized that Bharathram had a knack for the subject, and often solved well-known problems in an unconventional way. Bharathram inspired Birman to revisit a problem that had eluded her for decades: is the Burau representation — the translation of the structure of braids into algebraic objects called matrices — faithful for four-strand braids? This year, a 99-year-old Birman, Bharathram and collaborator Tara Brendle published their answer: yes.

The New York Times | 15 min read

Reference: arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed)

The concerns that researchers might outsource scientific judgement to generative artificial intelligence are valid, but aimed at the wrong object, argues computer scientist Marc Schmitt. The danger is not AI, but people’s assumption that chatbots are producing final answers. Users should treat AI tools as intellectual sparring partners, with which they can develop and hone their thinking. AI developers should encourage this argument-based dialogue with chatbots, and universities should treat a student’s ability to participate in these arguments as a core skill, Schmitt suggests.

Nature | 5 min read

To minimize the off-target effects of cancer therapies, researchers need to find ways to deliver drugs to tumours accurately. Some species of bacteria are attracted to the low-oxygen environment in tumours, which makes them ideal candidates to shuttle drugs directly to their target. These bacteria can also be engineered to manufacture the drug inside their cells, and even to sense the conditions of their environment to ensure that they only release their cargo inside a tumour.

Nature | 4 min video

This video is part of Nature Outlook: Drug delivery, an editorially independent supplement produced with financial support from Taiho Oncology, Inc.

rss_11_1789244493.title: AI researchers reckon with the $1.5 million ‘academia tax’
rss_11_1789244493.text:
Artificial-intelligence researchers say that the idea of leaving academia is tempting, but some nevertheless resist the move.Credit: Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty

If you’re looking to make money with your skills in artificial intelligence, academia isn’t the most lucrative destination. The National Bureau of Economic Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, conducted an analysis1 of AI researchers and identified those with similar specialisms across academia and the private sector. They found that the top 1% of industry authors earn US$1.5 million more per person every year than do their academic counterparts.

Nature spoke to academics, mostly in the United States and Europe, and many mentioned students who have gone to work for firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI, both in San Francisco, California, and earn millions of dollars a year. Despite that, those who remain in academia say that the freedom to choose their research and the joy of training the next generation trumps the increased salaries of industry, though many still gripe about the issues they face in finding stable funding streams.

Source: United States’ National Bureau of Economic Research

Increasingly, however, researchers are adopting hybrid roles in which they split their time between technology companies and university research, getting the benefits of both.

Here, 14 university academics who specialize in AI and computational science share their reasons for staying in academia and the factors that might push them into industry.

The freedom to choose

“I’m not yet convinced that the extra money is worth the loss of the ability to do research in the areas you find interesting in the long term. It’s a thing that you possibly don’t get in industry — in academia, you could have projects going for a decade.” — Stewart Clark, computational physicist at Durham University, UK

“As scientists and educators, academia gives us an unusual amount of freedom to decide what questions we want to work on and what we think matters. I think that’s tremendously powerful.” — Jian Ma, computational biologist at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania

“If I decide tomorrow to completely shift the area of research I’m working on, no one can stop me doing that. If you are in a company, it’s a completely different game. When you are leading an academic research laboratory, you are completely at the steering wheel and the freedom that you get there is very special.” — Dima Damen, computer scientist at the University of Bristol, UK, and at Google DeepMind.

Working and publishing openly

“A lot of people have bought into the idea that if you want to be on the cutting edge, you have to be at one of the big companies. But for me, I think it’s important that someone has the role of doing the work out in the open, reporting on experiments, reporting what works, what doesn’t and sharing artefacts that can be used by anyone to do scientific study or adaptation.” — Noah Smith, AI researcher at the University of Washington in Seattle

Mentoring the next generation

“The impact you can have from teaching is amazing. I still get e-mails from students from my early years of teaching. You get that more personal view of your impact on society.” — Ivor Simpson, informatics researcher at the University of Sussex in Brighton, UK

The professional advisers who can help you to move from academia to industry

“Three of my former PhD students are now faculty members. And I think that’s my greatest achievement, much more than research, because the research you do is going to be state-of-the-art today, but it’s not a legacy.” — Damen

“Seeing doctoral students progress is the key thing for me. When you’re holding meetings with them, they’re the experts and they know more than anybody else about the subject of their dissertation. And they go out into the world and make an impact. It’s a real pleasure to see that academics contribute to the world in this way.” — Gaurav Sukhatme, computer scientist at the University of Southern California, Los Angeles

It’s not just about money

“When I first moved back to academia, a lot of my friends from my PhD and from wider life were asking me why I was doing this. They said, ‘Are you mad? You’re losing a huge amount of salary.’ And this is something that obviously hasn’t recovered, because you don’t get paid very well as an academic. A lot of my undergraduates will go off and get paid more than I do, which is disappointing. However, I wanted my research to have impact beyond the generation of revenue. I think that that’s the main thing, as well as having a little bit more control over what it could be applied to.” — Simpson

“There are some roles in industry, such as managerial research and development, that are quite interesting. But I would say that I’ll think very carefully before trading the freedom I have to collaborate for a managerial role. Then you have to abandon science and I am enjoying it too much so far.” — Paola Carbone, computational chemist at the University of Manchester, UK

Leaving academia for industry? Here’s how to handle salary negotiations

“The amount of money that these guys are making at Anthropic and OpenAI is just mind‑boggling — from being my student two years ago to making US$2 million a year. Then again, they basically say, ‘If I have my job for five years, I’m going to be lucky’, because they see that they’re literally training the large language models that are going to replace them. So, they can see the end of the road.” — Peter Nugent, physicist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, California

“It’s definitely not all about the money. In my case, I think I can offer a unique perspective: I had the money. When I was working in investment banking, it was crazy; the hours are crazy. We have deadlines, and academics still have to work really hard, but the hours in banking were a different level.” — Vandana Dwarka, mathematician at Delft University of Technology, the Netherlands

rss_12_1789244495.title: Highly efficient base editing at PCSK9 and normal human embryo development
rss_12_1789244495.text: Cas9-based tools enable programmable DNA lesions for studying repair outcomes, gene function, and genome correction. In human embryos, Cas9-induced DNA double-strand breaks are genotoxic, causing frequent aneuploidy and large deletions1,2. Here, we evaluate DNA repair outcomes at nicks and mismatches introduced by base editors at the PCSK9 and HBG loci in human embryos. Delivering ABE8e-V106W as a protein at fertilization achieved editing at all PCSK9 alleles, supporting development to the blastocyst stage and the derivation of homozygous edited stem cell lines. No insertions or deletions were detected, although rare on-target chromosome breakage and chromosomal abnormalities occurred. Nevertheless, editing at bystander and off-target sites was mosaic, and the introduction of the editor as mRNA caused frequent embryo arrest due to guide-independent deaminase activity. Thus, unlike Cas9-induced DNA breaks, base editor-induced lesions are efficiently repaired. However, undesirable consequences for the genome and development can occur, currently precluding clinical use in reproduction.
